GeoGPT · Guided geology investigation

Which fossil names can we defend?

Can internal anatomy support a provisional identification for a carbonate-sediment census?

The geological task

A sediment census turns specimens into counts. Before interpreting those counts as environmental change, a geologist needs names supported by observable anatomy. Here you review one real CT specimen: the professional decision is to record a provisional identification or request better evidence. The Treatise supplies the anatomical criteria; the scan supplies the observations.

Your role: inspect the evidence and explain a bounded conclusion. GeoGPT performs the requested analysis. All required settings are already supplied.

Four useful words

Test
The foraminifer’s shell.

Chamber
One compartment within the shell.

CT section
A slice through the X-ray reconstruction.

Provisional
Useful for now, with its uncertainty stated.

The idea in plain language

A fossil name is a claim about anatomy. A whole-volume projection combines features at different depths; a CT section isolates one plane. Concentric bands may look persuasive, but the Treatise asks how chambers are arranged and connected. Compare those features before attaching a name. If the image does not resolve a feature, record it as unknown—not absent.

Execute the task rather than asking for intended use, validation purpose, thresholds, hypotheses, software, approval or other preferences. Ask only if a named input is missing or unreadable; name it and stop. Do not fabricate execution, observations or citations. Use short plain-language final answers, not JSON or a code dump. End with “Finished. Return to the handout.” Do not append a question or an offer. Use these attributed summaries of saved Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology entries. Nummulites: the description specifies an enrolled spiral sheet, with or without internal cavities; the illustrated median and transverse sections help interpret that coiled construction. Marginopora: a disc-shaped test with cyclic chambers, chamberlets connected by annular canals, and different main and lateral compartments. A test is the shell; a chamberlet is a small chamber subdivision; annular means ring-shaped. Both can have broadly circular outlines: silhouette alone is not decisive. Distinguish visible architecture from inferred microstructure. These two genera are comparison candidates, not an exhaustive identification key. Sources: https://forams.treatise.geolex.org/displayInfo.php?genera=Nummulites and https://forams.treatise.geolex.org/displayInfo.php?genera=Marginopora . These are teaching summaries, not verbatim diagnoses. Do not retrieve the CT specimen's published label. Inspect specimen-A-projection.png (three whole-volume projections). This investigation asks whether the available images justify putting this specimen into a named genus in a carbonate-sediment census, or referring it for closer inspection. Give only: (1) two visible shape observations, naming panels; (2) a two-row table naming the internal structure that would distinguish the candidates; (3) a provisional assessment, including “unresolved” if appropriate. Projections superimpose a volume; do not call them individual sections or assert invisible chamberlets. Describe light and dark regions without calling them holes, canals or other anatomical structures unless the image actually establishes that structure. Keep this assessment in the conversation for comparison. Do not ask the student to supply an identification key.
What you should see

Two observations and a two-row comparison of the internal evidence needed. “Unresolved” is an acceptable assessment.

3
Minutes 12–23

Use the Treatise to inspect the interior

Do this

Download the section image. Attach specimen-A-sections.png in the same conversation; confirm six panels in two rows. Send Prompt 2. Find each named panel in the image.

Why: Nummulites has an enrolled spiral sheet. Marginopora has cyclic chambers and a more detailed chamberlet-and-canal construction. A visible ring is not automatically proof of those fine connections. The reference tells us what to test, not what the image must show.

The Treatise criteria you are comparing

Nummulites: an enrolled spiral sheet. Look for evidence of continuous coiling through the sections.

Marginopora: cyclic chambers divided into chamberlets, connected by ring-shaped canals. A ring outline alone does not show these connections.

These are summaries of the saved Treatise entries linked below. The prompt already includes them. You do not have to construct or paste a morphology key. If a structure cannot be resolved, record it as unknown rather than absent.

Reading the reply: GeoGPT may call the central dark area an “umbilicus”. That anatomical interpretation is not established by a dark patch alone. Keep your own description as “central dark region”. The useful result here is the unresolved internal architecture and the reason to request better evidence.

Make and explain your decision

Do this

Tell your partner whether you would record a provisional genus or request more imaging. Point to the evidence and name one unresolved feature. Save or copy the final comparison from GeoGPT.

Why: Recording uncertainty is part of professional specimen review. A single selected specimen cannot measure general accuracy or determine geological age.

Research context and source papers

Current micro-CT research aims to classify foraminifera while preserving internal structure. This small exercise examines the evidence behind one identification; it does not reproduce an automated classifier or establish its accuracy.

The briefing above supplies what you need during class. These sources are for further study.

  • ForametCeTera: CT data and the classification problem
  • Treatise: Nummulites
  • Treatise: Marginopora
  • Original specimen dataset
